mechanism: Possible additive or variable modulation of glycemic control.
description: Preliminary human findings suggest concentrated acai supplements may alter fasting blood sugar alongside diabetes medications.
evidenceNote: NCCIH cautions that acai may increase or decrease fasting glucose with antidiabetes drugs.

mechanism: High trace manganese/iron content alters T1/T2 MRI signal intensity in the GI tract.
description: Concentrated acai pulp has paramagnetic properties that can interfere with the interpretation of gastrointestinal MRI scans.
evidenceNote: NCCIH advises telling your provider before a gastrointestinal MRI if using acai.

mechanism: Aconitine delays myocardial voltage-gated Na+ channel inactivation, triggering severe arrhythmias alongside antiarrhythmics.
description: Aconite alkaloids prolong cardiac sodium-channel activation and trigger polymorphic ventricular arrhythmias; combining with prescription antiarrhythmics (sodium/potassium channel blockers) risks fatal proarrhythmic collapse.

mechanism: Additive hypotension and autonomic instability.
description: Aconitine intoxication induces severe neurogenic and cardiogenic hypotension alongside malignant arrhythmias; concurrent blood pressure medications can accelerate circulatory collapse.

mechanism: Vagal and cardiac conduction depression alongside beta-blockade.
description: Aconitum alkaloids produce vagal stimulation, bradycardia, and refractory arrhythmias that can be dangerously compounded by beta-adrenergic blockade.

mechanism: Concomitant use with corticosteroids may increase the risk of potassium depletion or electrolyte imbalance, or alter immunological effects.
description: Combining anthraquinone stimulant laxatives (such as oral aloe latex or cascara) with systemic corticosteroids compounds potassium loss and increases the risk of hypokalemia and electrolyte imbalance. Consult a clinician before concurrent oral use.

mechanism: Hypokalemia enhances cardiac glycoside binding to myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase.
description: Oral anthraquinone aloe latex stimulant laxatives deplete intestinal and systemic potassium (hypokalemia), dangerously sensitizing the heart to digoxin toxicity and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias. (Applies to oral aloe latex; clear topical gel does not carry systemic anthraquinone laxative risk.)

mechanism: Thiazide-induced renal K+ excretion compounds anthraquinone-driven colonic potassium loss and secondary hyperaldosteronism.
description: Concomitant oral ingestion of anthraquinone-containing aloe latex with hydrochlorothiazide or other thiazide diuretics causes synergistic renal and intestinal potassium wasting, risking acute hypokalemia and cardiac arrhythmias. (This applies to stimulant aloe latex laxatives rather than clear topical inner-leaf gel.)

mechanism: Stimulation of pancreatic insulin synthesis and secretion alongside enhanced peripheral glucose utilization.
description: Oral aloe vera inner leaf preparations possess hypoglycemic properties that may compound insulin therapy, risking hypoglycemic episodes.

mechanism: Aloe vera may have antiplatelet effects that interact with anesthetic agents affecting coagulation.
description: A case of excessive intraoperative bleeding was reported in a patient taking aloe vera before surgery with sevoflurane anesthesia.
source: PubMed — Ann Pharmacother 2004: Possible interaction between sevoflurane and Aloe vera.

mechanism: Electrolyte-depletion proarrhythmia.
description: Hypokalemia from oral aloe latex sharply increases risk of arrhythmia with antiarrhythmic agents.

mechanism: Additive potassium wasting.
description: Oral aloe latex compounds corticosteroid-induced hypokalemia.

mechanism: Colonic potassium wasting potentiates cardiac glycoside inhibition of myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase.
description: Oral anthraquinone aloe latex stimulant laxatives deplete intestinal and systemic potassium (hypokalemia), dangerously sensitizing the heart to digoxin toxicity and fatal arrhythmias. (Applies to oral aloe latex; clear topical gel lacks anthraquinones.)

mechanism: Additive renal and colonic potassium excretion.
description: Oral aloe latex anthraquinones combined with thiazide or loop diuretics produce severe synergistic potassium loss and cardiac arrhythmias.

mechanism: Probable induction of hepatic CYP enzymes increasing S/R-warfarin clearance and lowering INR.
description: American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) significantly REDUCED warfarin anticoagulant effect (lowering INR and plasma warfarin concentration in a randomized placebo-controlled trial, Yuan et al. 2004), raising risk of arterial/venous thromboembolism. Avoid concurrent initiation/discontinuation without frequent INR monitoring.

mechanism: Potential cardiac glycoside sensitivity shift (including via potassium depletion or P-glycoprotein/inotropic effects) noted in regulatory safety warnings.
description: Co-administration with herbal products that affect cardiac rhythm, P-glycoprotein transport, or electrolyte balance may alter digoxin serum levels or sensitivity to digoxin toxicity. Confirm with your prescribing cardiologist or pharmacist before combining.

mechanism: Inhibition of platelet-activating factor (PAF) and thromboxane signaling.
description: Andrographolide inhibits PAF-mediated platelet aggregation in human and animal studies, potentially raising bleeding risk alongside warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, or clopidogrel.

mechanism: Andrographolide has vasodilatory properties and may lower blood pressure through multiple mechanisms.
description: Andrographis may have mild blood pressure-lowering effects that add to antihypertensive medications.

mechanism: Pharmacodynamic immunostimulation opposing calcineurin/corticosteroid immunosuppression.
description: Andrographis enhances immune-cell proliferation and cytokine production, potentially counteracting immunosuppressive medications in transplant recipients or autoimmune disease.

mechanism: Andrographolide inhibits PAF-induced platelet aggregation, adding to warfarin's anticoagulant effect.
description: Andrographis may have antiplatelet effects that increase bleeding risk with warfarin.

mechanism: Additive phototoxic skin reactions during UV exposure.
description: Furanocoumarins in angelica root sensitize skin to UV light; combining with photosensitizing drugs raises sunburn risk.
evidenceNote: Health Canada requires warning users to avoid prolonged UV exposure.

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet and coumarin-derived coagulation interference.
description: Angelica archangelica contains natural furanocoumarins that may add to bleeding risk or alter warfarin anticoagulation.
evidenceNote: Monograph literature flags ulcer/bleeding and coumarin cautions.

mechanism: Direct additive myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.
description: Dogbane contains cymarin and apocannoside cardiac glycosides producing lethal additive digitalis toxicity alongside digoxin.

mechanism: Hypokalemia-enhanced glycoside binding.
description: Potassium depletion from loop/thiazide diuretics greatly sensitizes the myocardium to cymarin cardiotoxicity.

mechanism: Potential interference with thyroid hormone replacement or thyroid function noted in regulatory safety guidance.
description: Compounds in horseradish (glucosinolate/isothiocyanate constituents) may influence thyroid function or iodine handling in susceptible individuals. Separate timing from levothyroxine and monitor thyroid function tests if advised by your clinician.

mechanism: Irreversible alkylation of platelet sulfhydryl groups by helenalin and 11-alpha,13-dihydrohelenalin inhibiting platelet aggregation.
description: Oral or concentrated systemic arnica preparations (non-homeopathic) contain helenalin sesquiterpene lactones that inhibit human platelet aggregation via thiol pathways, increasing bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
source: PubMed — Thromb Res 1990: Helenalin and 11 alpha,13-dihydrohelenalin, two constituents from Arnica montana L., inhibit human platelet function via thiol-dependent pathways.

mechanism: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase upregulation and mild potassium-sparing diuretic/choleretic actions.
description: Artichoke leaf extracts possess mild choleretic and blood pressure-lowering properties that may exert modest additive hypotensive effects alongside prescription antihypertensives.

mechanism: Choleretic stimulation modifying bile salt micelle formation and fat-soluble vitamin K absorption.
description: Dietary or supplemental artichoke components and vitamin K variability could theoretically influence anticoagulation stability; maintain consistent dosing and monitor INR.

mechanism: Additive myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.
description: Common milkweed contains cardenolide cardiac glycosides producing additive digitalis toxicity and fatal heart block with digoxin.

mechanism: Ashwagandha enhances natural killer cell activity and other immune parameters, opposing immunosuppression.
description: Ashwagandha has immune-stimulating properties that may counteract the effects of immunosuppressive medications.

mechanism: Ashwagandha may stimulate thyroid function by increasing T3 and T4 production, adding to exogenous thyroid hormone.
description: Ashwagandha may increase thyroid hormone production, potentially causing excessive thyroid levels in patients taking thyroid medication.

mechanism: Withanolides modulate GABA-A receptor signaling, producing additive CNS depression alongside benzodiazepine sedation.
description: Ashwagandha has mild sedative activity and may enhance the drowsiness, dizziness, and psychomotor impairment caused by lorazepam and other benzodiazepines.

mechanism: GABA-mimetic activity of withanolides augmenting central inhibitory neurotransmission.
description: Ashwagandha enhances central nervous system depression when combined with benzodiazepines, z-drugs, or barbiturates.

mechanism: Ashwagandha's withanolides show mild antiplatelet activity in vitro, and its thyroid-stimulating properties can change warfarin's protein binding and metabolism indirectly.
description: Limited evidence suggests ashwagandha may affect platelet aggregation and thyroid hormone levels, either of which can alter warfarin's effect. Monitor INR closely if combining them and keep ashwagandha dosing consistent.

mechanism: Astragalus polysaccharides stimulate immune cell proliferation and activity, opposing pharmacological immunosuppression.
description: Astragalus may counteract the immunosuppressive effects of cyclophosphamide while potentially reducing its side effects.

mechanism: Pharmacodynamic antagonism via dendritic cell and cytokine activation.
description: Astragalus stimulates T-cell/macrophage immune activity and may counteract therapeutic immunosuppression in organ transplant recipients or autoimmune diseases (NCCIH/MSK).

mechanism: Diuretic activity may reduce renal lithium clearance.
description: Astragalus may have mild diuretic effects that could affect lithium levels.

mechanism: Additive competitive muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonism across central and peripheral nervous systems.
description: Belladonna contains potent tropane alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine) that produce severe additive anticholinergic toxicity alongside prescription anticholinergic medications — risking acute delirium, urinary retention, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmia.

mechanism: Additive peripheral and central H1/muscarinic M1–M3 receptor blockade.
description: First-generation antihistamines share strong anticholinergic properties; taking them with belladonna risks synergistic drying, confusion, urinary retention, and dangerous CNS or cardiac toxicity.

mechanism: Muscarinic antagonism opposes elevated synaptic acetylcholine produced by cholinesterase inhibition.
description: Belladonna directly antagonizes cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, eliminating cognitive benefit and precipitating acute confusion in patients treated for dementia.

mechanism: Combined antimuscarinic receptor blockade by belladonna alkaloids and tricyclic antidepressants.
description: Combining belladonna alkaloids with tricyclic antidepressants causes dangerous additive muscarinic blockade, markedly increasing risks of tachycardia, paralytic ileus, blurred vision, and anticholinergic CNS toxicity.

mechanism: Bacoside A has demonstrated vasodilatory properties through calcium channel modulation.
description: Bacopa may have mild calcium channel blocking effects that add to antihypertensive medications.

mechanism: Competitive inhibition of human cytochrome P450 isoforms.
description: In-vitro studies reported by MSK indicate Bacopa extracts can inhibit CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19, potentially altering blood levels of narrow-margin prescription substrates.

mechanism: Synergistic acetylcholinesterase inhibition increasing synaptic acetylcholine.
description: Bacopa monnieri inhibits acetylcholinesterase and exhibits cholinomimetic activity, risking additive cholinergic side effects (nausea, bradycardia, sweating) alongside donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine.

mechanism: Stimulation of endogenous thyroid hormone synthesis/release compounding exogenous levothyroxine.
description: Preclinical evidence shows Bacopa monnieri can markedly increase thyroxine (T4) serum levels (~40%+ in animal models), risking thyrotoxicosis, palpitations, and arrhythmias when combined with prescription levothyroxine. Avoid combining or closely monitor TSH/free T4.

mechanism: Vitamin K antagonizes warfarin inhibition of VKORC1.
description: Barley grass and concentrated green-cereal powders contain substantial natural vitamin K; abrupt initiation or dose changes can antagonize warfarin and reduce INR (MSK).

mechanism: Theoretical additive antiplatelet or hepatic CYP/vitamin-K modulation.
description: Buchu extracts contain coumarin-related and polyphenolic constituents with limited preclinical data suggesting potential modulation of coagulation or antiplatelet drugs; monitor INR if taken near warfarin.

mechanism: Diuretic-mediated volume contraction promotes renal lithium retention.
description: Buchu exhibits traditional aquaretic/diuretic properties that can alter sodium and fluid balance, potentially reducing renal lithium excretion and increasing serum lithium toxicity risk.

mechanism: Berberine inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, dramatically reducing cyclosporine metabolism and efflux.
description: Berberine significantly increases cyclosporine blood levels (by nearly 100% in one study), increasing risk of toxicity.

mechanism: Berberine inhibits CYP2D6, which is the primary enzyme responsible for dextromethorphan metabolism.
description: Berberine may increase dextromethorphan blood levels by inhibiting its metabolism.

mechanism: Berberine inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 involved in losartan metabolism.
description: Berberine may increase losartan levels and its active metabolite, potentially enhancing blood pressure effects.
source: PubMed — Pharm Biol 2016: Effects of berberine on the pharmacokinetics of losartan and its metabolite EXP3174 in rat

mechanism: Both activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), creating additive hypoglycemic effects.
description: Berberine has similar blood sugar-lowering mechanisms to metformin. Combining them may cause excessive blood sugar reduction (hypoglycemia).
source: PubMed — Eur J Endocrinol 2012: A clinical study on the short-term effect of berberine in comparison to metformin on the metabolic characteristics of women with polycystic ovary syndrome.

mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition decreasing cyclosporine clearance.
description: Berberine — the major alkaloid in barberry bark/root — inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp and markedly raised blood cyclosporine concentrations (~34-75%) in human clinical studies, increasing nephrotoxicity.

mechanism: Human cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6, CYP3A4, CYP2C9) inhibition by berberine.
description: Repeated clinical dosing of berberine inhibited CYP2D6, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 activity in healthy human probe trials, risking elevated levels of sensitive prescription drugs.

mechanism: Transporter competition plus additive AMPK activation.
description: Berberine competes with metformin at organic cation transporters (OCT1/OCT2/MATE1) and exerts additive AMP-activated kinase glucose lowering; monitor glycemia and GI tolerance.

mechanism: Inhibition of platelet aggregation and potential additive antithrombotic effect.
description: Concentrated bilberry fruit anthocyanosides exhibit mild antiplatelet activity in preclinical/clinical models and may increase bruising or bleeding risk alongside warfarin or aspirin/antiplatelet agents. Monitor INR and bleeding signs.

mechanism: Synergistic antiplatelet action through dual inhibition of cyclooxygenase and platelet cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase.
description: Combining bilberry supplements with aspirin produces additive platelet antiaggregatory activity, prolonging bleeding time.

mechanism: Chromium and anthocyanin-mediated stimulation of peripheral glucose oxidation and glycolysis.
description: Bilberry leaf extract preparations possess active hypoglycemic properties that may cause additive blood glucose reductions with metformin.

mechanism: Inhibition of platelet aggregation and thromboxane A2 release compounding anticoagulant effects.
description: Anthocyanosides in bilberry exhibit antiplatelet properties and may augment hemorrhage risks when taken alongside warfarin.

mechanism: Bitter orange contains synephrine, an alpha-adrenergic agonist, and combining it with caffeine can add to stimulant effects.
description: Combining caffeine with bitter orange, another stimulant, can intensify caffeine's adverse effects, including tachycardia and seizures.

mechanism: Bitter orange inhibits CYP3A4 activity, which leads to increased blood levels of cyclosporine.
description: Bitter orange inhibits CYP3A4 and has been shown to increase blood levels of cyclosporine, so cyclosporine exposure may rise.

mechanism: Bitter orange inhibits CYP3A4 activity, which leads to increased blood levels of saquinavir.
description: Bitter orange inhibits CYP3A4 and has been shown to increase blood levels of saquinavir, so saquinavir exposure may rise.

mechanism: Both agents have independently been associated with hepatocellular injury; concurrent use may compound hepatic burden, though a direct interaction mechanism is unproven.
description: Rare cases of liver injury have been reported with black cohosh, and combining it with atorvastatin (which also carries hepatic risk) warrants liver function monitoring.

mechanism: Induction of intracellular protective antioxidants and interference with platinum-DNA adduct apoptosis.
description: Preclinical data indicates black cohosh extracts can attenuate the cytotoxic effectiveness of platinum-based antineoplastics like cisplatin.

mechanism: Weak-to-moderate hepatic CYP3A4/CYP2D6 inhibition observed in experimental systems.
description: In-vitro and MSK clinical monographs advise caution with drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 (and CYP2D6) while monitoring for clinical response or liver toxicity.

mechanism: Altered cellular chemosensitivity and CYP3A4 metabolism.
description: Preclinical oncology studies cited by MSK indicate black cohosh extracts increased cytotoxicity of doxorubicin and docetaxel but reduced cisplatin cytotoxicity — consult oncology team before concurrent use.

mechanism: Potential additive hepatotoxicity when combined with drugs that stress liver function.
description: Black cohosh has been associated with rare cases of liver damage. Combining with other hepatotoxic drugs may increase liver injury risk.

mechanism: Potential hepatic CYP modulation and additive idiosyncratic hepatocellular stress.
description: MSK warns that black cohosh may interact with simvastatin and other statins or hepatotoxic drugs, with rare reports of liver enzyme elevations when combined.

mechanism: Unclear mechanism; black cohosh may have selective estrogen receptor modulator-like activity.
description: Black cohosh may interact with tamoxifen in hormone-sensitive conditions. The nature of interaction is uncertain.
source: PubMed — Xenobiotica 2011: In vitro metabolic interactions between black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa) and tamoxifen v

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Concurrent use may alter platelet aggregation or anticoagulant response and elevate bleeding risk. Clinical monitoring (including INR checks when taking warfarin) and medical supervision are recommended before combining.

mechanism: Additive insulin-sensitizing and glucose-lowering effects.
description: Garlic preparations may modestly lower blood glucose, warranting glucose monitoring when combined with diabetes drugs.
evidenceNote: Health Canada advises consulting a health care practitioner if you have diabetes.

mechanism: Suspected intestinal CYP3A4 / P-glycoprotein induction decreasing protease inhibitor bioavailability.
description: Garlic supplements can markedly reduce blood concentrations of HIV protease inhibitors such as saquinavir, risking loss of viral control.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph explicitly warns patients taking protease inhibitors to consult a physician first.

mechanism: Organosulfur garlic constituents reduce platelet aggregation and add to anticoagulant activity.
description: Concentrated black or aged garlic extracts may potentiate anticoagulation and increase bleeding risk alongside warfarin.
evidenceNote: Health Canada garlic monograph mandates consulting a practitioner before use with blood thinners.

mechanism: Intestinal CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition by piperine.
description: Standardized piperine supplements may alter blood exposure to CYP3A4/P-gp substrates such as cyclosporine.
evidenceNote: Health Canada warns against combining therapeutic black pepper/piperine with medications without practitioner review.

mechanism: Piperine inhibits CYP enzymes, glucuronidation, and P-glycoprotein efflux, increasing oral bioavailability.
description: Piperine in black pepper can raise phenytoin blood concentrations and increase neurological side-effect risk.
evidenceNote: Health Canada black pepper monograph cites pharmacokinetic studies (Bano et al., Khajuria et al.) showing altered drug effectiveness.

mechanism: Inhibition of first-pass metabolism and P-gp transport enhances propranolol bioavailability.
description: Therapeutic piperine doses from black pepper significantly increase peak blood levels of propranolol, raising risk of bradycardia or dizziness.
evidenceNote: Clinical pharmacokinetic trials cited in Health Canada monograph documented elevated AUC/Cmax for propranolol.

mechanism: CYP1A2 and metabolic inhibition slows theophylline clearance.
description: Concentrated black pepper / piperine can raise blood levels of narrow-therapeutic-index theophylline, risking nausea, tremor, or tachycardia.
evidenceNote: Cited in Health Canada monograph warning that piperine may alter medication effectiveness (>25 mg/day fruit).

mechanism: Thymoquinone affects multiple CYP enzymes and may alter cyclosporine metabolism.
description: Black seed may interact with cyclosporine levels. Some studies suggest it may be protective, but monitoring is essential.

mechanism: Thymoquinone improves insulin sensitivity and may enhance pancreatic beta-cell function.
description: Black seed has blood sugar-lowering properties that may be additive with metformin.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Concurrent use may alter platelet aggregation or anticoagulant response and elevate bleeding risk. Clinical monitoring (including INR checks when taking warfarin) and medical supervision are recommended before combining.

mechanism: Additive insulin sensitivity and carbohydrate-absorption modulation.
description: Anthocyanin-rich Vaccinium leaf preparations may modestly reduce post-meal glucose alongside diabetes medicines.
evidenceNote: Monitor capillary blood glucose when starting concentrated blueberry-leaf extracts.

mechanism: Polyphenol and salicylate-like antiplatelet effects additive to warfarin.
description: High-dose Vaccinium blueberry extracts or leaf preparations may potentiate blood thinners and raise bruising or bleeding risk.
evidenceNote: Health Canada blueberry monograph warns before use if taking blood thinners above 5 g/day dried fruit equivalents.

mechanism: Potential additive hepatic stress in sensitive patients.
description: Because boldo contains ascaridole and carries hepatobiliary precautions, avoid pairing with hepatotoxic medications.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph requires consulting a clinician before use with liver or kidney disorders.

mechanism: Unknown pharmacokinetic or coumarin-related potentiation of vitamin K antagonists.
description: Boldo leaf extracts have been linked in clinical reports to elevated INR and potentiated warfarin anticoagulation.
evidenceNote: Supported by Health Canada monograph cautions and published warfarin-boldo INR case reports.

mechanism: Boswellic acids inhibit 5-lipoxygenase while NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, providing complementary anti-inflammatory pathways.
description: Boswellia may have additive anti-inflammatory effects with NSAIDs, potentially allowing NSAID dose reduction.

mechanism: Boswellic acids may inhibit platelet aggregation, adding to warfarin's anticoagulant activity.
description: Boswellia may have mild antiplatelet effects that increase bleeding risk with warfarin.

mechanism: Additive mild diuresis.
description: Oral burdock has a mild diuretic effect that can add slightly to fluid loss when taken alongside prescription diuretics.
evidenceNote: Health Canada requires labelling a potential diuretic effect.

mechanism: Additive hypoglycemic effect documented in herbal diabetes precautions.
description: Burdock preparations may lower blood glucose, calling for closer monitoring alongside metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin.
evidenceNote: Health Canada burdock monograph flags diabetic patients for practitioner review.

drugName: CYP3A4 Inducers (Rifampin, Carbamazepine, St. John's Wort)
mechanism: CYP3A4 induction accelerates bioactivation of pyrrolizidine alkaloids to hepatotoxic pyrrolic esters.
description: Drugs and herbs that INDUCE hepatic CYP3A4 (such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, phenobarbital, and St. John's wort) increase bioactivation of any residual unsaturated pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) in butterbur into reactive toxic pyrrole metabolites, markedly elevating liver-injury risk. Even PA-free butterbur products carry idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity warnings — avoid combining.

mechanism: Mild central depressant effects observed in high-dose preclinical screening models.
description: Systemic or high-dose internal calendula preparations may theoretically enhance drowsiness when combined with prescription sedatives; topical cosmetic use does not share this concern.

mechanism: Additive CNS depression mediated by isoquinoline alkaloids.
description: California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) enhances alcohol-induced drowsiness, slowed reflexes, and impaired coordination.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph instructs avoiding alcohol or drowsiness-causing products while using California poppy.

mechanism: Cumulative GABAergic / CNS depressant sedation.
description: Concurrent benzodiazepines or prescription analgesics and California poppy produce excessive daytime sedation and fall hazard.
evidenceNote: Health Canada warns against combining with analgesics or products that cause drowsiness.

mechanism: Hypokalemia-induced ventricular repolarization instability.
description: Anthraquinone-induced hypokalemia increases risk of life-threatening arrhythmias alongside antiarrhythmic and QT-prolonging drugs (EMA Section 4.5).

mechanism: Additive mineralocorticoid and colonic potassium depletion.
description: Systemic corticosteroids increase renal potassium loss; combining with senna pods compounds hypokalemia and electrolyte depletion risk.

mechanism: Hypokalemia-potentiated myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase toxicity.
description: Senna/Cassia acutifolia anthraquinone glycosides can cause hypokalemia when overused (>1 week), dangerously increasing risk of digoxin toxicity and lethal cardiac arrhythmias (EMA).

mechanism: Additive potassium wasting.
description: Concurrent use compounds renal and intestinal potassium wasting, risking acute hypokalemia, muscle weakness, and cardiac arrhythmias.

mechanism: Antiplatelet, calcium-channel vasodilatory, and weak CYP3A4 inhibition.
description: Cat's claw inhibits platelet aggregation and may lower blood pressure, risking additive bleeding or hypotension; it also inhibits CYP3A4 in vitro.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: There are theoretical reasons to suspect that cat’s claw might interact with anticoagulant, antiplatelet, and blood pressure drugs, and other supplements as well. If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using cat’s claw or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Hirsutine and other alkaloids have calcium channel blocking properties.
description: Cat's claw may have mild blood pressure-lowering effects that are additive with antihypertensives.

mechanism: Inhibition of cytochrome P450 3A4-mediated oxidation by pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids.
description: Cat's claw inhibits CYP3A4 enzymes and can alter the pharmacokinetic profile and blood concentrations of protease inhibitors.

mechanism: Oxindole alkaloids stimulate interleukin and tumor necrosis factor release, opposing calcineurin inhibition.
description: Cat's claw stimulates immune cell activity and may counteract the therapeutic immunosuppression achieved by cyclosporine.

mechanism: Oxindole alkaloids in cat's claw enhance phagocytosis and stimulate T-cell and B-cell proliferation.
description: Cat's claw stimulates immune function and may counteract immunosuppressive medications.

mechanism: Immunostimulatory pharmacodynamic antagonism.
description: Uncaria tomentosa (cat's claw) stimulates immune cytokine/lymphocyte signaling and may counteract immunosuppressive medications (NCCIH/MSK).

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet activity combined with local gastrointestinal mucosal irritation.
description: Oral cayenne supplements may irritate the gastric mucosa and exert additive antiplatelet effects when taken with aspirin, increasing the risk of stomach irritation or bleeding.

mechanism: ACE inhibitors accumulate bradykinin and substance P in the airways while capsaicin directly activates TRPV1 sensory C-fibers to release substance P.
description: Capsaicin from cayenne sensitizes airway cough receptors and can worsen dry cough triggered by ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril or enalapril, even with topical formulations if inhaled or transferred.

mechanism: Capsaicin-mediated attenuation of platelet aggregation and altered arachidonic acid signaling alongside vitamin-K-antagonist anticoagulation.
description: Concentrated oral cayenne supplements contain capsaicinoids that may decrease platelet aggregation and enhance fibrinolysis, increasing bleeding risk when combined with warfarin.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Interactions between chamomile and some drugs metabolized by the liver and warfarin (a blood thinner) have been reported, and there are theoretical reasons to suspect that chamomile might interact with other drugs as well, such as sedatives. If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using chamomile or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Apigenin and related flavonoids inhibit platelet aggregation and COX activity, adding to aspirin's irreversible platelet inhibition.
description: Chamomile (apigenin) has mild antiplatelet activity and may add to aspirin's blood-thinning effect. Case reports describe bleeding with heavy chamomile use alongside anticoagulant therapy.

mechanism: Apigenin binding to central benzodiazepine receptors producing additive somnolence with psychotropic drugs.
description: Chamomile possesses mild central nervous system depressant and anxiolytic actions that can enhance drowsiness when combined with SSRIs.

mechanism: Chamomile constituents may inhibit CYP3A4, reducing cyclosporine metabolism.
description: Chamomile may increase cyclosporine levels through enzyme inhibition.

mechanism: Potential hormonal or metabolic interaction with estrogen/progestin oral contraceptives noted in official regulatory monograph cautions.
description: Chamomile might have some of the same effects as estrogen. Preliminary studies suggest that taking chamomile along with birth control pills might decrease the effects of birth control pills. In addition, chamomile might worsen any condition that is sensitive to exposure to estrogen, such as breast or uterine cancer. Consult a healthcare practitioner before use if taking oral contraceptives or hormone-containing medications.

mechanism: Mild GABA-A / benzodiazepine-receptor binding by apigenin causing additive CNS depression.
description: German chamomile (Matricaria recutita) contains apigenin and mild CNS-depressant constituents that may produce additive drowsiness or sedation when combined with prescription sedatives, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or sleep medications. Exercise caution with driving or alertness.

mechanism: Coumarin constituents in chamomile may have mild anticoagulant activity and inhibit platelet aggregation.
description: Chamomile contains coumarin compounds that may enhance warfarin's anticoagulant effect. Cases of bleeding have been reported.

mechanism: Flavonoid constituents may suppress platelet aggregation and thromboxane signaling, complementing aspirin's irreversible COX-1 blockade.
description: Concentrated Roman chamomile extracts may mildly inhibit platelet aggregation and add to aspirin's antiplatelet effect, increasing the likelihood of bruising or bleeding.

mechanism: Suspected inhibition of CYP3A4-mediated cyclosporine metabolism in the gut wall and liver.
description: Chamomile preparations may alter hepatic and intestinal drug-metabolizing enzymes, potentially increasing blood concentrations and toxicity risk of cyclosporine. Consult a transplant specialist before use.

mechanism: Flavonoid ligands such as apigenin and luteolin show affinity for central GABA-A / benzodiazepine binding sites, producing additive sedation.
description: Roman chamomile may have mild sedative properties and could enhance drowsiness or central nervous system depression when combined with benzodiazepines, sleep medications, or other CNS depressants.

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet and coumarin-derived anticoagulant potential, alongside possible inhibition of hepatic CYP enzymes involved in warfarin clearance.
description: Roman chamomile contains coumarin-related and flavonoid constituents that may add to the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and increase bleeding risk. Monitor INR closely and avoid concentrated preparations unless supervised by a clinician.

mechanism: Additive myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.
description: Wallflower contains cheirotoxin cardiac glycosides adding directly to digoxin cardiotoxicity.

mechanism: Additive hepatocellular toxicity risk.
description: Greater celandine (Chelidonium majus) is a documented cause of acute hepatocellular injury; avoid combining with hepatotoxic medications.
evidenceNote: LiverTox assigns Celandine Likelihood Score B (uncommon but likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury).

mechanism: Concomitant use with corticosteroids may increase the risk of potassium depletion or electrolyte imbalance, or alter immunological effects.
description: Over a dozen publications, largely from Europe, have described clinically apparent acute liver injury attributable to greater celandine (Chelidonium majus). Liver injury typically arises after 1 to 6 months, with jaundice and moderate to marked elevations in serum aminotransferase levels. The pattern of injury is usually hepatocellular and the clinical presentation and liver histology resemble acute viral hepatitis. Immunoallergic features are uncommon, but autoantibodies may be present in low to moderate levels in many cases. The clinical syndrome, however, rarely resembles autoimmune hepatitis and usually resolves rapidly once the botanical is discontinued and without need of corticosteroid therapy. There have been no reports of greater celandine hepatotoxicity from the United States or the Americas. Consult a physician or pharmacist before combining with systemic corticosteroids.

mechanism: Overlapping hepatotoxicity without additive therapeutic benefit.
description: Combined greater celandine and hepatotoxic immunosuppressants like methotrexate elevates risk of severe transaminase elevation and jaundice.
evidenceNote: Backed by LiverTox Score B acute liver injury cases.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Concurrent use may alter platelet aggregation or anticoagulant response and elevate bleeding risk. Clinical monitoring (including INR checks when taking warfarin) and medical supervision are recommended before combining.

mechanism: Exogenous vitamin K reverses warfarin inhibition of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).
description: Chlorella naturally contains significant vitamin K1, which can antagonize warfarin and reduce INR anticoagulation stability.
evidenceNote: Health Canada Chlorella monograph requires blood-thinner consultation at >=250 mg/day or >=6 mcg vitamin K/day.

mechanism: P-glycoprotein transport inhibition decreasing digoxin elimination.
description: Quinine and quinidine markedly elevate serum digoxin concentrations (~2-fold for quinidine) by inhibiting renal/biliary P-glycoprotein clearance, causing severe digoxin toxicity.

mechanism: hERG/IKr potassium-channel blockade compounding ventricular repolarization delay.
description: Quinine and quinidine in cinchona bark prolong cardiac QT interval; combining with Class IA/III antiarrhythmics or QT-prolonging drugs risks fatal torsades de pointes.

mechanism: Additive clotting-factor depression and CYP inhibition.
description: Cinchona alkaloids (quinine/quinidine) inhibit hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and CYP metabolism, potentiating warfarin hypoprothrombinemia and hemorrhage.

mechanism: P-gp inhibition decreasing digoxin clearance.
description: Quinine/quinidine increases plasma digoxin concentration via P-gp inhibition, risking digitalis intoxication.

mechanism: Synergistic cardiac IKr/hERG blockade.
description: Quinine/quinidine in Cinchona calisaya prolong QT and risk fatal torsades de pointes alongside QT-prolonging medications.

mechanism: Additive insulin-mimetic signaling and glucose uptake.
description: Concentrated cinnamon supplements may lower fasting blood glucose and cause additive hypoglycemia alongside insulin or sulfonylureas (NCCIH).

drugName: Hepatotoxic Drugs (Cassia Cinnamon High Coumarin Exposure)
mechanism: Additive hepatic injury from Cassia coumarin exceeding EFSA 0.1 mg/kg TDI.
description: Cassia cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia / C. aromaticum) contains high levels of coumarin, a hepatotoxin that can compound liver injury risk when combined with hepatotoxic drugs (acetaminophen, statins, amiodarone, methotrexate).

mechanism: Coumarin in cassia cinnamon is hepatotoxic in susceptible individuals, creating additive risk with hepatotoxic drugs.
description: Cassia cinnamon (high coumarin) combined with hepatotoxic medications may increase liver damage risk.

mechanism: Cinnamon polyphenols improve insulin sensitivity through GLUT4 transporter activation, complementing metformin's AMPK activation.
description: Cinnamon may enhance blood sugar-lowering effects of metformin. Beneficial but requires monitoring.
source: PubMed — J Hum Reprod Sci 2017: The Effect of Metformin and Cinnamon on Serum Anti-Mullerian Hormone in Women Having PCOS:

description: Concurrent use may alter platelet aggregation or anticoagulant response and elevate bleeding risk. Clinical monitoring (including INR checks when taking warfarin) and medical supervision are recommended before combining.

mechanism: Inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4 first-pass metabolism and OATP uptake.
description: Citrus bioflavonoids such as naringin and hesperidin can inhibit intestinal CYP3A4 and OATP transporters, altering calcium-channel blocker levels.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph advises asking a health care provider before combining with medications.

mechanism: Flavonoid-mediated CYP/transporter modulation and mild antiplatelet effects.
description: Concentrated citrus bioflavonoids (>=50 mg/day) may alter drug metabolism or platelet function alongside blood thinners.
evidenceNote: Health Canada 2026 monograph requires practitioner consultation if taking medications including blood thinners.

mechanism: Synergistic COX / thromboxane inhibition.
description: Concentrated eugenol / clove supplements taken alongside aspirin or antiplatelets add to mucosal and antiplatelet bleeding risk.
evidenceNote: Concentrated clove extracts warrant caution unlike normal culinary spice amounts.

mechanism: Eugenol blocks thromboxane A2 synthesis and arachidonic acid-induced platelet aggregation.
description: Concentrated clove oil or eugenol supplements can inhibit platelet aggregation and raise bleeding risk with warfarin.
evidenceNote: High-dose eugenol is flagged in LiverTox for early coagulation abnormalities.

mechanism: Potential additive natriuretic/diuretic effect.
description: Combining herbs with traditional diuretic activity alongside prescription diuretics could theoretically amplify fluid loss or electrolyte shifts.

mechanism: Mild diuretic-induced sodium/water loss can increase proximal tubular lithium reabsorption.
description: Traditional diuretic use of stone root (Collinsonia) could theoretically reduce renal lithium clearance and elevate serum lithium into a toxic range, similar to other botanical diuretics. Confirm with a prescriber before combining.

mechanism: Immunostimulant or immunomodulatory botanicals may theoretically oppose the therapeutic action of immunosuppressive medications.
description: Immune-modulating botanical or colostrum supplements may theoretically counteract immunosuppressive medications or unpredictably alter immune activity in transplant or autoimmune therapy. Consult your specialist before use.

mechanism: Synergistic hepatocellular glutathione depletion and endothelial sinusoidal injury.
description: Oral comfrey contains hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids capable of causing veno-occlusive liver injury; avoid with acetaminophen or hepatotoxic drugs.
evidenceNote: LiverTox assigns oral Comfrey Likelihood score C and notes oral products are restricted due to sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Hepatotoxicity from comfrey is now rare, as it is widely accepted as being toxic when taken internally and oral formulations are restricted or banned in most countries. Management should be directed at limiting further injury and specific treatment of complications (ascites, variceal bleeding). Anticoagulants have not been shown to be beneficial. Difibrotide (a complex mixture of single stranded DNA prepared from pig intestine) has recently been approved for therapy of severe SOS accompanied by renal or pulmonary failure occurring after myeloablation for hematopoietic cell transplantation. More extensive description of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and its management are given in the introductory section and in discussion of the antineoplastic alkylating agents. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: CYP3A4/CYP2B6 induction increases bioactivation of pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
description: Enzyme inducers accelerate conversion of comfrey pyrrolizidine alkaloids into reactive toxic pyrrole metabolites in the liver.
evidenceNote: Bioactivation mechanism well described in LiverTox hepatotoxicity literature.

mechanism: Pregnane X receptor (PXR) activation inducing CYP3A4 transcription.
description: Guggulsterones activate human PXR and induce CYP3A4 gene expression in vitro/hepatocytes, potentially lowering levels of CYP3A4-metabolized drugs (MSK).

mechanism: Increased thyroid peroxidase and triiodothyronine (T3) generation.
description: Guggulsterones stimulate thyroid iodine uptake and conversion in preclinical/clinical settings and may alter thyroid hormone requirements.

mechanism: Decreased gastrointestinal absorption and PXR/CYP3A4 induction.
description: Human clinical pharmacokinetic trial showed guggulsterone/guggul reduced bioavailability and plasma AUC of both propranolol and diltiazem significantly, risking reduced cardiovascular efficacy (MSK).

mechanism: Additive suppression of central respiratory drive during peripheral neuromuscular ventilatory failure.
description: Poison hemlock induces ascending skeletal-muscle and diaphragmatic paralysis; adding opioids, benzodiazepines, or sedatives accelerates hypoventilation and fatal respiratory arrest.

mechanism: Synergistic presynaptic and postsynaptic blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate.
description: Coniine in poison hemlock acts as a curare-like nicotinic acetylcholine antagonist at the neuromuscular junction; co-exposure with surgical neuromuscular blockers causes catastrophic prolonged respiratory paralysis.

mechanism: Additive myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.
description: Lily of the valley contains convallatoxin cardiac glycosides causing lethal additive digitalis toxicity when combined with prescription digoxin.

mechanism: Hypokalemia sensitizes myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase to convallatoxin.
description: Diuretic-induced hypokalemia sensitizes the heart to convallatoxin-induced fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

mechanism: May alter blood pressure or interact additively/antagonistically with antihypertensive therapy according to regulatory monograph warnings.
description: Coenzyme Q10 may modestly lower blood pressure and add to the hypotensive effect of antihypertensive medications, increasing the risk of dizziness or low blood pressure. Monitor blood pressure when starting or adjusting.

mechanism: Cordycepin and adenosine may inhibit platelet aggregation.
description: Cordyceps may have mild antiplatelet effects that increase bleeding risk with anticoagulant medications.

mechanism: Platelet aggregation inhibition without primary PT/aPTT change.
description: Cordyceps militaris/sinensis extracts inhibit ADP- and collagen-induced platelet aggregation and may increase bleeding risk alongside anticoagulants or antiplatelets (MSK).

mechanism: Cordyceps polysaccharides stimulate natural killer cells and macrophages, potentially opposing immunosuppression.
description: Cordyceps has immune-modulating properties that may interfere with immunosuppressive medications.

mechanism: Cytokine and immune-cell modulation.
description: Cordyceps exhibits immunomodulatory properties that may theoretically interfere with immunosuppressive regimens in transplant or autoimmune patients (MSK).

mechanism: Potential pharmacodynamic or serotonergic interaction with antidepressant medications noted in official monograph safety guidance.
description: Do not use yohimbe if you are taking types of antidepressant medications called monoamine oxidase inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants. Yohimbe can interact with these medications. If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using yohimbe or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Consult a prescribing clinician before combining with SSRIs, SNRIs, or other serotonergic antidepressant medications.

mechanism: Potential sympathomimetic or serotonergic interaction with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) documented in regulatory safety warnings.
description: Do not use yohimbe if you are taking types of antidepressant medications called monoamine oxidase inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants. Yohimbe can interact with these medications. If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using yohimbe or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Avoid concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of discontinuing MAOI therapy.

mechanism: Urinary acidification altering renal clearance and passive non-ionic reabsorption kinetics of urinary excreted antibiotics.
description: Cranberry juice may slightly alter urinary acidification and tubular reabsorption kinetics of beta-lactam antibiotics such as amoxicillin.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: There is conflicting evidence about whether cranberry interacts with the anticoagulant (blood thinner) warfarin. If you take warfarin or any other medicine, talk with your health care provider before using cranberry or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Weak modulation of organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATP) and intestinal CYP3A4 by cranberry components.
description: High-dose cranberry consumption may alter the intestinal absorption and systemic exposure of lipophilic statins like atorvastatin.

mechanism: Potential modulation of intestinal CYP3A4 / P-glycoprotein transport.
description: Cranberry juice/extracts have been associated with altered tacrolimus pharmacokinetics/blood concentrations in clinical case reports cited by NCCIH; transplant patients should monitor tacrolimus trough levels.

mechanism: Cranberry flavonoids may inhibit CYP2C9, slowing warfarin metabolism. The interaction appears dose-dependent and more significant with cranberry juice concentrate.
description: Cranberry products may increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. Several cases of increased INR and bleeding have been reported, including one fatality.
source: PubMed — Nutrients 2021: Bidirectional Influences of Cranberry on the Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Warf

mechanism: Additive suppression of platelet aggregation and thromboxane A2 synthesis alongside aspirin's irreversible COX-1 inhibition.
description: Concentrated curcumin may enhance aspirin's antiplatelet effect and prolong bleeding time. Watch for unusual bruising or bleeding and stop at least 2 weeks before surgical procedures.

mechanism: Dual antiplatelet inhibition plus potential modulation of CYP enzymes (CYP3A4 / CYP2C19) and piperine-related bioavailability interactions.
description: High-absorption curcumin extracts may add to clopidogrel's antiplatelet effect and could alter hepatic prodrug activation, increasing bleeding risk or unpredictable response.

mechanism: Improved insulin sensitivity and hepatic gluconeogenesis suppression via AMPK activation.
description: Curcumin supplementation may lower blood glucose levels and add to metformin's hypoglycemic effect; monitor blood sugar closely to adjust therapy if needed.

mechanism: Inhibition of intestinal ABCG2 (BCRP) and P-glycoprotein efflux transporters increases oral sulfasalazine absorption.
description: Curcumin has been shown in human pharmacokinetic studies to substantially increase blood levels of sulfasalazine, raising the risk of systemic adverse effects.

mechanism: Inhibition of intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein reduces tacrolimus first-pass clearance.
description: Case reports indicate concentrated curcumin or turmeric products (especially with piperine) can raise blood tacrolimus levels and precipitate nephrotoxicity in transplant recipients.

mechanism: Curcuminoids inhibit platelet aggregation and CYP2C9/CYP3A4 warfarin metabolism, while piperine-enhanced formulations further boost systemic curcumin and drug exposure.
description: Bioavailability-enhanced curcumin extracts can potentiate warfarin's anticoagulant effect and increase bleeding risk. Avoid combining or obtain close INR monitoring from your prescriber, and discontinue before surgery.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: There are theoretical reasons to suspect that dandelion might interact with antidiabetes, anticoagulant, antiplatelet, and water pill drugs, among others. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Mineral content and fiber in dandelion may chelate ciprofloxacin and reduce gastrointestinal absorption.
description: Dandelion may reduce ciprofloxacin absorption, potentially decreasing antibiotic effectiveness.

mechanism: Diuretic effect reduces renal lithium clearance, elevating serum lithium concentrations.
description: Dandelion's diuretic properties may decrease lithium excretion, increasing blood levels and risk of lithium toxicity.

mechanism: Negative chronotropic and calcium-channel/electrophysiologic modulation.
description: Animal/MSK pharmacology indicates harpagoside extracts may affect heart rate, cardiac rhythm, and blood pressure; monitor patients taking antiarrhythmics or antihypertensives.

mechanism: Increased gastric acidity plus mucosal irritation.
description: Devil's claw stimulates gastric acid secretion and carries warnings against use with NSAIDs or peptic ulcers due to compounded GI irritation and ulcer bleeding risk.

mechanism: Harpagoside may have antiplatelet activity and potentially affect warfarin metabolism.
description: Devil's claw may affect blood clotting and interact with warfarin therapy.

mechanism: Possible CYP2C9 inhibition and additive antiplatelet/hemorrhagic effects.
description: Case report and MSK/NCCIH advisories document purpura and elevated INR when devil's claw was added to warfarin; avoid or monitor INR closely.

description: Concurrent exposure to foxglove cardiac glycosides and beta-blockers produces additive slowing of AV node conduction, risking profound bradycardia, high-grade heart block, and syncope.

mechanism: P-glycoprotein inhibition increases circulating glycosides alongside synergistic AV nodal depression.
description: Verapamil and diltiazem reduce renal/P-glycoprotein clearance of digitalis glycosides and add AV-nodal depression, raising plasma glycoside toxicity and heart-block risk.

mechanism: Mineralocorticoid-mediated potassium depletion potentiates Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition by cardiac glycosides.
description: Systemic corticosteroids promote renal potassium loss; combined with foxglove cardiac glycosides, hypokalemia sharply raises the risk of digitalis arrhythmia and toxicity.

mechanism: Additive inhibition of myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase raising intracellular calcium and automaticity.
description: Purple foxglove contains digitoxin and digoxin-like cardiac glycosides; combining any foxglove preparation with prescription digoxin causes direct additive cardiac glycoside overdose, hyperkalemia, and fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

mechanism: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia enhance glycoside binding to myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase.
description: Potassium-wasting loop and thiazide diuretics deplete serum potassium and magnesium, dramatically sensitizing the myocardium to digitalis toxicity and fatal cardiac arrhythmias even at low glycoside exposure.

description: Dong quai contains coumarin compounds and may prolong bleeding time, adding to aspirin's antiplatelet effect. Use caution, especially before surgery.

mechanism: Potential phytoestrogenic, dopaminergic, or endocrine receptor interaction with hormone replacement therapy noted in regulatory monograph warnings.
description: Constituents with phytoestrogenic, selective estrogen-receptor, or CYP-modulating activity may alter hormone balance or compete with exogenous estrogen/progestin hormone replacement therapy. Review with your prescriber before combining.

mechanism: Potential hormonal or metabolic interaction with estrogen/progestin oral contraceptives noted in official regulatory monograph cautions.
description: Constituents with endocrine, phytoestrogenic, or CYP hepatic enzyme effects could theoretically alter estrogen/progestin activity or breakthrough bleeding risk alongside combined oral contraceptives. Consult a pharmacist or prescriber.

mechanism: Coumarins in dong quai have inherent anticoagulant activity, and the herb may also inhibit platelet aggregation.
description: Dong quai may significantly enhance anticoagulant effects of warfarin. Cases of markedly elevated INR have been documented.

mechanism: Echinacea's immunostimulatory effects oppose the immunosuppressive mechanism of corticosteroids.
description: Echinacea may partially counteract the immunosuppressive effects of corticosteroids.

mechanism: Echinacea activates macrophages and T-cells, directly opposing cyclosporine's immunosuppressive mechanism.
description: Echinacea's immune-stimulating properties may counteract the immunosuppressive effects of cyclosporine, risking organ rejection.

mechanism: Echinacea might increase cytochrome P450 activity, thereby reducing levels of drugs metabolized by these enzymes.
description: Echinacea might increase cytochrome P450 activity, which could reduce levels of some drugs metabolized by these enzymes.

mechanism: Echinacea polysaccharides and alkamides stimulate macrophage activity, cytokine production, and T-cell function, pharmacologically opposing immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and corticosteroids.
description: Echinacea stimulates immune activity and may counteract immunosuppressive therapy, raising the risk of organ rejection in transplant recipients and reducing drug efficacy in autoimmune disease.

mechanism: Immune stimulation may oppose methotrexate's immunosuppressive action. Both may affect liver function.
description: Echinacea may interfere with methotrexate's immunosuppressive effects and potentially increase hepatotoxicity risk with prolonged use.

mechanism: Immune stimulation counteracts pharmacological immunosuppression.
description: Echinacea may reduce the effectiveness of tacrolimus by stimulating the immune system that tacrolimus is designed to suppress.

mechanism: Mild inhibition of hepatic CYP1A2 enzyme activity.
description: Echinacea extracts may modestly inhibit CYP1A2 metabolism, slightly prolonging caffeine jitters or insomnia.
evidenceNote: Referenced alongside pharmacokinetic enzyme-inhibition studies of Echinacea preparations.

mechanism: Immunostimulatory cytokine modulation counteracting calcineurin inhibition plus mild CYP3A4 interaction potential.
description: Immune-stimulating Echinacea angustifolia can theoretically oppose immunosuppressants used after transplant or for autoimmune disease.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph requires consulting a practitioner if taking immunosuppressants or with autoimmune disease.

mechanism: Antagonism of therapeutic immunosuppression.
description: Do not combine Echinacea angustifolia with tacrolimus without transplant specialist approval due to opposing immune effects.
evidenceNote: Grounded in Health Canada immunosuppressant contraindication/precaution statement.

mechanism: Pharmacodynamic antagonism of immunosuppressive therapy.
description: Echinacea pallida should not be paired with cyclosporine without physician oversight because immune stimulation opposes immunosuppression.
evidenceNote: Health Canada monograph mandates practitioner consultation if taking immunosuppressants.

description: Immune-modulating botanical or colostrum supplements may theoretically counteract immunosuppressive medications or unpredictably alter immune activity in transplant or autoimmune therapy. Consult your specialist before use.

mechanism: Opposing immune-pathway activation.
description: Avoid unsupervised Echinacea pallida during tacrolimus therapy because herbal immune stimulation conflicts with graft protection.
evidenceNote: Directly supported by Health Canada Echinacea pallida monograph warnings.

mechanism: Additive diuresis.
description: Elder bark preparations carry a recognized diuretic effect that can add subtly to loop or thiazide diuretics.
evidenceNote: Health Canada requires warning consumers of possible diuretic effect.

mechanism: Anthocyanins may improve insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake.
description: Elderberry may have mild blood sugar-lowering effects that could add to diabetes medication effects.

mechanism: Elderberry increases cytokine production (IL-1 beta, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8) and activates immune cells, opposing pharmacological immunosuppression.
description: Elderberry stimulates the immune system and may counteract immunosuppressive medications used after organ transplant or for autoimmune conditions.

mechanism: Eleutherosides may cross-react with digoxin immunoassay, leading to falsely elevated serum digoxin levels.
description: Eleuthero may interfere with digoxin level monitoring, causing falsely elevated readings on some assays.

mechanism: Some eleutherosides may affect platelet aggregation pathways.
description: Eleuthero may have mild effects on platelet function that warrant monitoring with warfarin.

mechanism: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction opposes vasodilator and antihypertensive therapy.
description: Ephedra causes systemic vasoconstriction and blood-pressure elevation, directly antagonizing blood-pressure lowering medications.

mechanism: Additive sympathomimetic stimulation across cardiac beta and alpha adrenergic receptors.
description: Concurrent ephedra and stimulants such as caffeine markedly increase heart rate, blood pressure, palpitations, and seizure risk.
evidenceNote: NCCIH explicitly warns against theoretical and clinical stimulant stacking with caffeine.

mechanism: Sympathomimetic catecholamine surge lowers cardiac arrhythmia threshold in digitalis-treated patients.
description: Ephedrine alkaloids increase myocardial irritability and the likelihood of arrhythmias when combined with digoxin.
evidenceNote: Clinical toxicology profiles of ephedra document serious palpitations and cardiac events.

mechanism: Potential interference with thyroid hormone replacement or thyroid function noted in regulatory safety guidance.
description: Ephedra alkaloids exert strong sympathomimetic stimulation that can compound thyroid hormone cardiac effects, increasing the risk of tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, and nervousness alongside levothyroxine. Avoid combining.

mechanism: Inhibition of norepinephrine breakdown compounds ephedrine-induced catecholamine release.
description: Combining ephedrine alkaloids with MAOIs can precipitate fatal hypertensive crisis, hyperpyrexia, intracranial hemorrhage, and cardiac arrhythmias.

mechanism: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction counteracts antihypertensive therapy; unopposed alpha stimulation can raise blood pressure.
description: Ephedra opposes blood-pressure-lowering drugs and may trigger acute hypertension when paired with beta-blockers.
evidenceNote: NCCIH identifies people with cardiovascular conditions as being at elevated risk with ephedra.

mechanism: Ephedrine releases stored norepinephrine while MAOIs block catecholamine breakdown, causing dangerous sympathetic surge.
description: Combining Ephedra sinica (ephedrine alkaloids) with monoamine oxidase inhibitors can provoke severe hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, and stroke.
evidenceNote: NCCIH notes ephedra alkaloids carry serious cardiovascular risks including hypertension, stroke, and myocardial infarction.

mechanism: Synergistic alpha/beta-adrenergic sympathetic stimulation and phosphodiesterase inhibition.
description: Concurrent ephedra and caffeine or sympathomimetic stimulants markedly increases risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures, tachycardia, and sudden death.

mechanism: Prostaglandin E1-mediated antiplatelet inhibition.
description: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) inhibits platelet aggregation via prostaglandin E1 and may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners (NCCIH).

mechanism: GLA/prostaglandin E1 excess sensitizing epileptogenic foci alongside D2-blocking phenothiazines.
description: Case reports cited by NCCIH and clinical toxicology warn that combining evening primrose oil with phenothiazine antipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold and trigger temporal-lobe epilepsy/seizures.

mechanism: GLA in evening primrose oil may reduce seizure threshold, and phenothiazines also lower seizure threshold, creating additive risk.
description: Evening primrose oil may lower the seizure threshold, increasing seizure risk in patients taking phenothiazines.

mechanism: GLA and its metabolites may inhibit platelet aggregation.
description: Evening primrose oil may have mild anticoagulant properties that add to warfarin's effect.

mechanism: Cation complexation and reduced fluoroquinolone dissolution/permeation in the presence of aqueous fennel constituents.
description: Concomitant oral administration of fennel markedly reduces the intestinal absorption and peak plasma concentration of ciprofloxacin by chelation and gastric transit changes; separate doses by at least 2 hours.
source: PubMed — J Pharm Pharmacol 1999: Effect of oral administration of fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) on ciprofloxacin absorption and disposition in the rat.

mechanism: Weak estrogen receptor binding by trans-anethole and photoanethole metabolites.
description: Concentrated fennel extracts contain trans-anethole and phytoestrogenic compounds that could theoretically compete with or modulate estrogen receptor signaling.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: Despite being widely used, fenugreek has not been implicated in cases of clinically apparent liver injury and, in prospective studies, has had no effect on serum enzyme levels. In vitro studies have demonstrated hepatoprotective activity of fenugreek extracts in several animal models. Because of the high fiber content, estrogenic and coumadin-like effects of fenugreek, it has a potential to cause herb-drug interactions particularly if taken in high doses with antiplatelet drugs and warfarin. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Additive hypoglycemic effects through insulin secretion stimulation and improved insulin sensitivity.
description: Fenugreek may enhance blood sugar-lowering effects of sulfonylureas, increasing hypoglycemia risk.

mechanism: 4-Hydroxyisoleucine in fenugreek directly stimulates insulin secretion and improves insulin sensitivity.
description: Fenugreek may enhance the blood sugar-lowering effect of insulin, increasing hypoglycemia risk.

mechanism: Coumarin derivatives in fenugreek may have additive anticoagulant activity.
description: Fenugreek contains coumarin compounds that may enhance warfarin's anticoagulant effect.
source: PubMed — Pharmacotherapy 2001: Potential interaction between warfarin and boldo-fenugreek.

mechanism: Parthenolide blocks platelet aggregation and granule secretion through mechanisms distinct from aspirin's COX inhibition, producing an additive effect.
description: Feverfew (parthenolide) inhibits platelet aggregation and serotonin release from platelets, adding to aspirin's effect and increasing bleeding risk.

mechanism: Both feverfew and NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, creating additive antiplatelet effects.
description: Feverfew may have additive antiplatelet effects with NSAIDs, potentially increasing bleeding risk.

mechanism: Parthenolide inhibits platelet aggregation and may affect prostaglandin synthesis, adding to warfarin's anticoagulant activity.
description: Feverfew may increase bleeding risk when combined with warfarin due to antiplatelet effects.

mechanism: Potential additive antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity, or altered anticoagulant metabolism noted in official regulatory safety guidance.
description: There are theoretical reasons to suspect that flaxseed or flaxseed oil might interact with other drugs, such as anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs. If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using flaxseed, flaxseed oil, or other herbal products; some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways. Consult a healthcare professional and monitor coagulation parameters (such as INR or bleeding signs) when combining with anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.

mechanism: Additive suppression of platelet aggregation.
description: High-dose flaxseed oil may add minor antiplatelet activity alongside low-dose aspirin or NSAIDs.
evidenceNote: NCCIH advises discussing flaxseed oil with a clinician when using antiplatelet medicines.

mechanism: Theoretical additive antiplatelet effect.
description: Combined flaxseed oil and antiplatelet medications like clopidogrel may increase easy bruising or nosebleeds.
evidenceNote: NCCIH cautions about antiplatelet co-administration.

mechanism: Theoretical additive antiplatelet/omega-3 fatty acid effects alongside vitamin K antagonism.
description: Flaxseed oil and lignans may enhance bleeding tendency or alter clotting parameters when paired with anticoagulants.
evidenceNote: NCCIH notes theoretical reasons flaxseed or flaxseed oil might interact with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs.

mechanism: Additive acute hepatocellular injury and HLA-linked idiosyncratic toxicity.
description: Fo-ti (Polygonum multiflorum) carries LiverTox Likelihood Score A for severe hepatitis; avoid co-use with hepatotoxic drugs.
evidenceNote: LiverTox identifies Polygonum multiflorum as a well-established cause (Score A) of clinically apparent liver injury including fatal cases.

mechanism: Additive hepatic metabolic burden.
description: Co-administering Polygonum multiflorum with statins raises baseline liver-enzyme elevation and cholestatic/hepatocellular risk.
evidenceNote: Documented high LiverTox hepatotoxicity signal.

mechanism: Hypokalemia-enhanced proarrhythmia.
description: Electrolyte depletion from cascara laxative use increases arrhythmia risk alongside antiarrhythmic medications (EMA Section 4.5).

mechanism: Concomitant use with corticosteroids may increase the risk of potassium depletion or electrolyte imbalance, or alter immunological effects.

The onset of injury is usually within 1 to 8 weeks of starting regular use of kratom powder or tablets, with symptoms of fatigue, nausea, pruritus and dark urine followed by jaundice. The pattern of liver injury is typically cholestatic or mixed, and it can be severe with serum bilirubin levels rising above 20 mg/dL. The severe cholestasis can be accompanied by acute renal failure and bone marrow toxicity. Fever is common, but not rash or eosinophilia and autoantibodies are usually absent. The cholestasis can be prolonged, but usually resolves spontaneously. Corticosteroids as well as N-acetylcysteine have been used in cases of suspected kratom hepatotoxicity, but their efficacy is unproven. Kratom is a banned substance in many areas of the country and considered an agent of abuse rather than a dietary supplement. At least two dozen cases of clinically apparent liver injury with jaundice have been reported in the literature and a similar number reported to the Food and Drug Administration adverse event database. Consult a physician or pharmacist before combining with systemic corticosteroids.

description: In multiple small, short term placebo-controlled trials of Lingzhi or Reishi, serum aminotransferase levels did not change during treatment, and there were no reported instances of clinically apparent liver injury or jaundice. Furthermore, Lingzhi and Reishi are not listed in the many reviews of causes of liver injury from herbal and dietary supplements. Nevertheless, there have been a small number of reports from China, Japan, Thailand, and India of clinically apparent liver injury attributed to Lingzhi or Reishi or their extracts. The latency to onset was typically 1 to 2 months, but ranged from a few days to as long as 6 months, presenting with symptoms of fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, poor appetite, dark urine, and jaundice. In published cases, the liver injury has been hepatocellular and immune allergic reactions (fever, rash) were not common. In some instances, low levels of autoantibodies were found but immunoglobulins were typically normal and liver biopsies were more suggestive of drug induced liver injury than autoimmune hepatitis. Severity in published cases ranged from mild and asymptomatic elevations in serum aminotransferase levels to clinically apparent hepatitis and even severe hepatitis with hepatic failure. Recovery was rapid once the herbal product was stopped and complete within 1 to 3 months with or without corticosteroid therapy. There have been no reports of chronicity. Many of the cases were poorly documented and the attribution to Ganoderma species somewhat weak. In some cases, other common causes of liver injury were not excluded (such as gallstones, acetaminophen overdose, exposure to other herbal products, contaminants of the herbal product). In view of the extensive worldwide use of Ganoderma lucidum and Lingzhi, clinically apparent liver injury from its use must be extremely rare. Consult a physician or pharmacist before combining with systemic corticosteroids.
